newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Veneer of normalcy masks Cambodia rights abuses. [CORRECTED 10:27 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Veneer of normalcy masks Cambodia rights abuses. [CORRECTED 10:27 GMT]

text.p: Nine days after a violent coup shook Phnom Penh, Cambodia's capital has the bustle of a city verging on normality. Traffic is heavy, banks and businesses are opening and battle damage is being repaired.
But Western officials warn that beneath the veneer lie fear, political unrest and serious human rights abuses.
"For those people who care about Cambodia this is the time of greatest risk, when the country seems to be getting back to normal," explained a Western official who asked not to be named.

"Meanwhile prisoners are being killed, opposition figures have fled or are in hiding and newspapers and radio stations have stopped work. The danger is that Cambodians and the outside world can be persuaded to accept the status quo."
Cambodia's First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh was ousted over the weekend of July 5-6 and his troops routed by forces loyal to Second Prime Minister Hun Sen.
The two formed an uneasy coalition government after U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993, and tensions and political violence had been increasing over recent months.

Western officials said on Monday said that at least 25 persons captured in the fighting and its aftermath had died, among them a secretary of state at the Interior Minister and Ranariddh loyalist Ho Sok. (Corrects position).
Based on witnesses' accounts, the officials said some prisoners were being tortured prior to execution.

The message has not been lost on publishers, journalists or Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party workers, who fear for their lives and refuse to rely on Hun Sen's promise that Cambodia remains a pluralistic, democratic country.
FUNCINPEC's radio station was trashed in the fighting. Two opposition journalists associated with Ho Sok have either fled or been arrested.
A dozen FUNCINPEC newspapers, funded either directly or through friendly advertising, have closed down, as have about a half-dozen other papers affiliated with opposition parties.
This despite Hun Sen's televised, post-coup pledge to respect freedom of the press during an address in which he encouraged the opposition to resume publishing.

Critics say that Hun Sen, having driven Prince Ranariddh and FUNCINPEC troops from the capital, now wants to clothe himself in the mantle of democratic respectability by encouraging a thoroughly cowed and de-fanged opposition.
Some say fear has paralysed publishers and journalists in Phnom Penh. Others characterise the pause as prudent behaviour.
So long as the jury remains out on Hun Sen's true intentions the effect is rampant self-censorship in a city which had a flourishing opposition press only two weeks ago.

"What you have is a bunch of newspapers which could publish in theory but which are declining to publish in fact, for whatever reason," said Mike Fowler, an American journslist who has worked as an adviser to Cambodian journalists.
Ranariddh is jetting from one world capital to the next trying to garner support for his vanished government.
A number of his top political and military advisers are dead or captured and the bulk of the troops still loyal to him are retreating into the jungles of northwestern Cambodia.
Less certain of their status are mid-level and junior supporters of the prince who find themselves stranded in Phnom Penh, where politics has suddenly become a deadly game.

Five young men who think of themselves as patriots and democrats came out on the losing side in the recent fighting. They have been hiding at a "safe house" in the capital, trying to arrange passage out of the country.
None is a soldier. Several are Youth Party workers who basked in the reflected glow of Ranariddh before he fled the capital on July 4, the day before the fighting started.
Their most prized possessions are snapshots of themselves with the prince at various Youth Party functions.
Mere extras in a political tragedy, they now fear for their lives.
"We are afraid and we want to leave the country but we have no money and no embassy seems willing to help us," said 22-year old Ta.

"We hear rumours of some of our friends being arrested and we see what we think are policemen outside our homes, but it is difficult to get good information. We think it is safer to hide for now than to risk disappearing."
